findings.headline: Future energy efficiency and net-zero regulatory requirements create unquantified additional cost exposure beyond the £239m estimate.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that future Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards, EPC requirements, and net-zero expectations may exceed current investment capacity or technical feasibility. These are emerging and uncertain, but represent potential unbudgeted demand that could crystallise as regulatory requirements.
findings.matters: The £239m figure does not appear to include full contingency for future-proofing against uncertain regulatory costs. If tighter energy standards are enforced, the council may face either accelerated borrowing, reserve depletion, or non-compliance.
findings.figures: Future requirements unquantified; not clearly itemised within £239m base estimate
findings.quote: Future MEES, EPC and net-zero expectations may exceed current investment capacity or technical feasibility.

findings.headline: Delivery capacity constraints across internal teams and contractors threaten programme timescales and cost containment.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges material constraints in programme delivery, contract management, and specialist services, alongside variability in contractor performance. These constraints create risk that capital programmes will slip or cost more than planned.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver capital programmes at planned pace allows inflation to compound during delivery, increases finance costs if programmes extend, and creates operational disruption that may affect resident satisfaction and complaints.
findings.figures: Identified constraints in internal delivery model; no quantified estimate of cost/delay impact
findings.quote: There are constraints in programme delivery, contract management and specialist technical areas, alongside variability in contractor performance, access issues and coordination challenges across multiple workstreams.

findings.headline: External cost and interest-rate pressures create material risk to HRA financial headroom and borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: The council's own risk register names inflation, materials availability, and interest rates as factors reducing HRA headroom. This is not a theoretical concern — it is flagged as a key strategic risk that could force the council to either increase borrowing, defer programmes, or draw on reserves.
findings.matters: Erosion of HRA headroom by external factors constrains the council's ability to absorb cost overruns, respond to compliance failures, or maintain investment programmes. It increases the risk profile for any lender or creditor.
findings.figures: Risk identified affecting unquantified HRA headroom; external factors reducing financial flexibility on £239m programme
findings.quote: Investment needs exceed available resources. External factors (inflation, materials, interest rates) reduce HRA headroom.

findings.headline: Rising construction and maintenance costs are compressing HRA headroom as capital budgets face inflation pressure.
findings.detail: The council identifies rising construction and maintenance costs as an active pressure on the HRA, coinciding with new energy efficiency requirements and decarbonisation obligations. This means the real purchasing power of available capital budgets is shrinking even as identified need grows.
findings.matters: Unchecked cost inflation erodes the council's ability to complete planned programmes within budget, either forcing programme delays (increasing future costs) or increasing HRA borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: Unquantified inflationary pressure on £239m estimated cost base
findings.quote: The Council is facing growing financial pressures within the HRA, alongside rising construction and maintenance costs and emerging requirements relating to energy efficiency and decarbonisation

findings.headline: Investment needs of £239m over 30 years far exceed what the HRA can afford to deliver.
findings.detail: The stock condition survey identifies a 30-year investment requirement of approximately £239m, with significant concentrated pressure in the first five years (£56m-£66m depending on section), but the council explicitly states it cannot deliver everything at once. Investment will be phased based on what is affordable within HRA constraints, forcing difficult choices between safety/compliance, energy improvements, and long-term sustainability.
findings.matters: A structural gap between identified maintenance need and available funding creates long-term asset deterioration risk, potential compliance failures, and pressure to either increase borrowing or defer spending into cost-escalating future years.
findings.figures: £239m (or £238.8m) over 30 years; £56m-£66m in first five years; £46,208 per home over 30 years
findings.quote: The scale of investment needed across the housing stock exceeds what can be delivered within available resources, and the stock condition survey identifies approximately £239m over 30 years, including significant investment pressures in the early years.

findings.headline: Service quality deterioration: Q4 complaint escalation at 23%, 70% repairs-related, with 76% of stage-2 complaints still justified
findings.detail: Quarter four saw sustained high complaint volumes with 23% escalation rate, indicating issues not resolved at first stage. 70% of complaints centred on repairs (damp, mould, heating). Critically, 76% of stage-two complaints were still justified, showing root causes remain unaddressed and leading to increased compensation costs (£65k paid at Stage 1).
findings.matters: High complaint escalation and unresolved service failures suggest operational fragility in core housing services. Risk of regulatory intervention (Ombudsman, Consumer Standards) and escalating compensation costs.
findings.figures: 23% escalation rate, 70% repairs complaints, 76% of stage-2 complaints justified, £65,000 compensation paid at stage 1
findings.quote: Quarter four also saw the highest level of escalation, with an overall escalation rate of 23%, indicating that issues were not consistently resolved at the first stage. Complaints continued to be dominated by repairs, which accounted for 70% of all cases

findings.headline: Void losses reached £449k (1.46% of potential rent income) on 10% increase in property turnover
findings.detail: Total void losses for year: £449,266. The number of properties turned over was 256, a 10% increase on prior year, indicating higher tenant churn. This combines with £577k shortfall in dwelling rent income, suggesting underlying tenant affordability or housing demand pressures.
findings.matters: Void losses and elevated tenant turnover are barometers of housing demand stress and affordability pressures in the district. Rising churn rates can signal deteriorating income sustainability.
findings.figures: £449,266 total void loss, 1.46% of potential rental income, 256 properties turned over (10% increase on prior year), £577k rent income shortfall
findings.quote: Void losses were higher than anticipated, there were some delays getting tenants into new properties which resulted in lower rental income being charged against original estimates.

findings.headline: Revenue reserves fell to 8.1% of rent income (below 10% target) and major repairs reserve completely exhausted to zero
findings.detail: HRA Revenue Reserve is now £2.6m (8.1% of annual rent income) against the 10% target of £3.27m. More critically, the Major Repairs Reserve which opened at £5.196m is now at nil balance after being fully drawn to fund major works. Future major repairs will be funded by borrowing rather than reserves, increasing debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: Reduced reserve buffers limit the HRA's ability to absorb operational shocks. Shift to borrowing for major repairs increases ongoing Capital Financing Requirement and debt burden on the account.
findings.figures: £2.6m revenue reserves at 8.1% of rent income vs 10% target (£3.27m), Major Repairs Reserve £0 (from £5.196m)
findings.quote: Revenue reserves are £2.6m, which is 8.1% of rent income, slightly below the target of 10%...the carried forward balance of £5.2m was utilised, resulting in a nil closing balance.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law (damp/mould compliance) drove £460k in-house works and £299k unbudgeted agency staffing
findings.detail: New statutory requirement to fix serious hazards including damp and mould within strict timelines created unexpected demand surge. Council responded with £460k on equipment and in-house works, and £299k on temporary agency staff during winter period to handle compliance workload.
findings.matters: New regulatory requirement creates ongoing unpredictable cost pressures that may continue into future years. Suggests HRA budgets may not adequately anticipate emerging compliance demands.
findings.figures: £460,000 equipment and in-house works, £299,000 agency staff costs
findings.quote: £460,000 was the result of in-house works and equipment purchased to reduce the cost of external contractors. The introduction of Awaab's Law has had a significant impact on the service over the winter period, placing clear timelines on response and investigation requirements.

findings.headline: £993,000 adverse variance: budgeted £616k surplus became £377k deficit, requiring reserve draw-down
findings.detail: The HRA's financial position deteriorated significantly from budget. Key drivers were £1.5m higher repairs spending, £577k shortfall in dwelling rent from void losses, and £299k additional agency staff costs. Partially offset by £1.3m savings on debt and interest. Revenue reserve balance drawn down from £3.023m to £2.646m.
findings.matters: Represents a material swing in HRA financial position. Signals operational issues (particularly in repairs and voids) were not anticipated in budget-setting and suggests potential ongoing pressures.
findings.figures: £616,000 budgeted surplus, £377,000 outturn deficit, £993,000 adverse movement
findings.quote: The HRA budget for 2025/26 was set with an overall surplus of £616,000, this report highlights an overall deficit of £377,000, a downwards movement of £993,000.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs reduced to £20,000 deficit from £180,000 pressure through prevention activity
findings.detail: Despite average TA cases being 262 against a budget of 254, overspend was limited to £20,000 through strengthened prevention activity and support for move-on accommodation. However, the council notes this requires continued monitoring; TA cases have since reduced to 180 at report writing, but this remains a volatile demand area.
findings.matters: While successfully managed in 2025/26, homelessness and TA costs remain volatile and subject to rapid changes in demand; future cost pressures are possible if prevention activity falters
findings.figures: £180,000 TA cost pressure; reduced to £20,000 deficit after mitigation; TA cases 262 vs budget 254; since reduced to 180
findings.quote: There was a pressure of £180,000 relating to homelessness costs with the average number of Temporary Accommodation cases increasing to 262 compared to a budget assumption of 254. However, strengthened prevention activity, improved support for move-on accommodation and the more robust application of the legislative framework have helped to manage and contain these pressures in year

findings.headline: Long-term investment portfolio remains £329,000 below original investment value despite improvements
findings.detail: The council holds £29.7m in long-term investments but the portfolio value remains £329,000 below the original amount invested. While improving steadily since covid impacts, the council notes this position limits ability to exit funds without crystallising losses, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: The council has significant capital locked into underperforming investments with limited exit flexibility; this reduces available liquid resources for emergencies or opportunities
findings.figures: £29.7m total investment portfolio; £329,000 below original investment value; improved £748,000 in year
findings.quote: The overall portfolio is below the original investment value by £329,000 and has been steadily improving year on year since significant reductions in capital values as a result of the covid pandemic. This position does limit the ability to exit funds without crystallising losses overall

findings.headline: £4.7m transferred to Port Health reserve to cover Border Facility operational risks
findings.detail: The council transferred £4.7m into a dedicated Port Health reserve to cover future risks associated with operating the Border Facility post-Brexit. This large transfer reflects uncertainty about the facility's operational sustainability and potential income risks.
findings.matters: A £4.7m reserve requirement signals significant operational risk and income volatility in a key council service; any shortfall would draw heavily on reserves
findings.figures: £4.7m transferred to Port Health reserve; Ashford Port Health reserve now £5.518m
findings.quote: £4.7m Transfer of Port Health funds to Port Health reserve, to cover future risks associated with the operation of the Border Facility

findings.headline: Facilities Management overspent by £431,000 on business rates for partially occupied Civic Centre
findings.detail: Increased business rates on the Civic Centre drove a £431,000 overspend in Facilities Management. The Civic Centre remains only partially occupied by AMC and DVSA, limiting eligibility for business rates relief. The council is progressing removal from rates following the April 2026 transfer of the CCTC Operating Centre.
findings.matters: The council has a significant asset (Civic Centre) that is underutilised and generating unexpected costs; asset strategies may not be aligned with operational needs
findings.figures: £431,000 Facilities Management pressure; partly driven by business rates on partially occupied Civic Centre
findings.quote: Facilities Management – There was an in-year pressure of £431.000, primarily reflecting increased business rates. This is driven by the continued partial occupation of the Civic Centre by AMC and DVSA, limiting eligibility for reliefs, alongside the revaluation of Council occupied floors at International House.

findings.headline: Corporate Management Costs overspent by £609,000 due to unbudgeted pay award of £412,000
findings.detail: Pay negotiations with Unison resulted in salary costs rising by £412,000 above budget. Additionally, the salary savings target of £110,000 was not transferred from services as in previous years. Together these accounted for most of the Corporate Management Costs overspend of £609,000.
findings.matters: Pay pressures exceeding budget indicate wage inflation outpacing council assumptions, creating ongoing budget risks in future years
findings.figures: £609,000 Corporate Management Costs deficit; £412,000 pay award pressure; £110,000 salary savings target not transferred
findings.quote: Corporate Management Costs had a deficit of £609,000, reflecting a £412,000 increase in salary costs above those estimated when the budget was set following negotiations with Unison. The salary savings target of £110,000 was also not transferred from services as in previous years.

findings.headline: Kent Business Rates Pool ending after 2025/26, removing £1.966m annual benefit
findings.detail: The council's participation in the Kent Business Rates Pool provided £1.966m in net benefit in 2025/26 by reducing levy payments. The pool will cease in 2026/27 because the business rates reset removes growth benefits that pooling depends on. The council will lose this saving entirely.
findings.matters: Loss of £1.966m in annual pooling benefit is a material reduction in retained business rates income that will require offsetting savings or reserves use in future years
findings.figures: £1.966m net benefit in 2025/26; pool ends 2026/27; Ashford retained 30% of pool growth
findings.quote: The benefit of pooling is that the levy paid to Government is significantly lower than if the Council had acted individually, this has resulted in an estimated net benefit to Ashford of £1.966m in 25/26... The pool will not continue in 26/27 due to the business rates reset removing the growth benefit

findings.headline: Business Rates declined by £2.559m due to successful appeals reducing billable value
findings.detail: Business Rates revenue fell significantly due to successful ratepayer appeals and reductions in Empty Premises relief. This resulted in a £1.177m deficit on the Collection Fund for business rates, with Ashford's share being £471,000. This is a structural reduction in billable value, not a temporary collection issue.
findings.matters: Appeals-driven reductions in the business rates base are permanent and indicate lower sustainable revenue from this source going forward
findings.figures: £2.559m reduction in Business Rates billed; £1.177m Collection Fund deficit; £471,000 Ashford's share
findings.quote: The in year deficit is made up of a reduction of Business Rates billed of £2.559m, this is largely due to a number of successful appeals which has reduced the billable value, as well as an increase in Empty Premise relief issued.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate fell to 96.5% from 97.0%, with resistance to payment increasing
findings.detail: Council Tax collection declined year-on-year. The council attributes this to cost-of-living pressures, empty homes premiums, and increased resistance to payment including 'Freemen of Land' claims. Court date delays are also slowing recovery action, pushing more debt collection into the following financial year.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates combined with active resistance suggest the council may struggle to realise forecast Council Tax income in future years, affecting both revenue and cash flow timing
findings.figures: 96.5% 2025/26 vs 97.0% 2024/25; collection rates have fallen
findings.quote: The final in-year collection rates for 2025/26 were 96.5% for Council Tax and 97.0% for Business Rates (2024/25 rates of 97.0% and 97.1% respectively). While Business Rate collection is broadly in line with last year, Council Tax collection has dropped, it is thought this is due to external factors, particularly economic climate such as cost of living generally, empty homes premiums and increased resistance to paying council tax, e.g. 'Freemen of Land'.

findings.headline: Bad debt provision increased by £231,000 due to economic conditions making debt harder to recover
findings.detail: The Finance directorate overspent by £617,000, with £231,000 of this driven by an increase in corporate bad debt provision. The council attributes this to ongoing economic conditions making debt recovery more difficult. This signals deteriorating payment behaviour across the council's debtors.
findings.matters: Growing bad debt provisions indicate weakening creditworthiness among the council's debtors and suggest revenue collection may become increasingly challenged
findings.figures: £231,000 increase in bad debt provision; Finance deficit of £617,000
findings.quote: Finance had an overall deficit of £617,000 in 2025/26 which included an increase in the corporate bad debt provision by £231,000. This was increased due to ongoing economic conditions which is making debt harder to recover

findings.headline: External auditor made Key Recommendation on HRA Medium Term Financial Sustainability
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's Value for Money report published in February 2025 identified one Key Recommendation relating to HRA Medium Term Financial Sustainability. Progress was reported to the Audit Committee on 17 March 2026, with overall good progress noted and the council expecting the recommendation to be discharged in the 2025-26 VFM report.
findings.matters: HRA financial sustainability concerns indicate potential financial risks in the council's Housing Revenue Account and whether it can sustain service delivery without drawing down reserves or requiring subsidy from the general fund.
findings.quote: The most recent VFM report was published in February 2025. One Key Recommendation was made relating to HRA Medium Term Financial Sustainability

findings.headline: Housing service control weaknesses from high staff turnover, though new management has been installed to implement remediation
findings.detail: The council identifies high turnover in Housing staff as resulting in lack of continuity and low-level control, creating control environment risk. However, management notes new management are now in post and procedures are being implemented to address the gaps.
findings.matters: Housing services (including temporary accommodation and subsidy fraud risk areas) are flagged by the council as having been under-controlled; a lender needs assurance that control weaknesses in income-critical services are remediating
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: No, however the high turnover of Housing staff is still resulting in lack of continuity and low-level control. New management are now in post and procedures are being implemented.

findings.headline: Contingent liabilities from Virgin Media and Thurrock cases remain unresolved, plus Elwick Place Phase 2 liability continuing past building completion
findings.detail: The council has multiple contingent liabilities disclosed in the accounts (Note 42). Virgin Media and Thurrock cases are ongoing. The Phase 2 Elwick Place contingent liability is of particular concern as it persists even after the building phase has been completed, suggesting an unresolved claim or obligation.
findings.matters: Unquantified contingent liabilities represent potential future financial exposure; a lender needs visibility of the council's legal and contractual risks that could crystallise into actual liabilities affecting financial position
findings.figures: None quantified in this document
findings.quote: See note 42 Contingent liabilities where we are mentioning the Virgin media case and the Thurrock case. In 2025/26 we will reconsider Including Phase 2 Elwick Place as the contingent liability still exists after the building phase has passed.

findings.headline: ABC subsidiary forecasting £650,000 General Fund deficit driven by property voids, grant funding cuts, and pay award overspend
findings.detail: Q3 budget monitoring for ABC (a council subsidiary) forecasts an overall General Fund deficit of £650k. Environment/property services under pressure from property voids causing lower rental income and service charge collection. Finance team facing bank charge increases and reduced grant funding from Kent County Council. Corporate management overspent because the annual pay award was settled at 5% but had only been budgeted at 3%.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand financial pressures in council subsidiaries; a £650k deficit in a subsidiary reduces available funds for the group and indicates potential cash flow challenges and loss-making operations
findings.figures: £650,000 forecast General Fund deficit; pay award settled at 5% vs 3% budgeted
findings.quote: As per ABC's normal business - Q3 Budget monitoring report forecasts an overall deficit to the General Fund (GF) of £650,000 driven by: Environment property and recreation – there is a pressure in this area due to property voids, therefore lower rental income and service charges, Finance is showing a pressure due to bank charges increases and reduction in grant Funding from KCC, and Corporate Management is showing a pressured driven by the increase in the annual pay award which was budgeted for at 3% but settled at 5%.

findings.headline: Infinity property development project materially impaired in subsidiary due to planning delays, inflation, war-driven borrowing costs, and regulatory changes
findings.detail: The Infinity project in A Better Choice for Property Development Ltd (a council subsidiary where the council is lender) has been impaired. Initial planning was blocked by Natural England's nutrient level ruling. Once that resolved, the project faced hyper-inflation, elevated borrowing costs from the Ukraine war, and additional Building Safety Regulator compliance costs (Grenfell-related, for buildings over 18m). Construction costs have risen way beyond the Gross Development Value, making the scheme unviable. The site could only realise £1.5m if marketed, substantially below original expectations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand material losses in the council's property subsidiary and the council's exposure as lender; this represents a significant capital deterioration and raises questions about the viability of the council's development strategy
findings.figures: £1,500,000 estimated market value of site if development does not proceed; construction costs described as 'way beyond GDV Values'
findings.quote: The Infinity project, held within A Better Choice for Property Development Ltd (a subsidiary of A Better Choice for Property Ltd and part of the wider ABC Group), has been impaired due to significant economic and regulatory pressures impacting scheme viability...All theses factors have led to a significant increase in construction costs (way beyond GDV Values) which have materially reduced the viability of the scheme, resulting in an impairment being recognised in the Company's financial statements.

findings.headline: Triennial pension fund actuarial valuation in 2025/26 will refresh all assumptions; net liability stands at £11 million but underlying assets and liabilities are large (£147.6m and £158.9m).
findings.detail: The council will undertake a triennial revaluation of the local government pension scheme liability in 2025/26. The net liability as at 31 March 2025 was £11 million, but the underlying pension fund assets were £147.6 million and liabilities £158.9 million. The triennial valuation means actuarial assumptions will be fully refreshed rather than rolled forward, 'which increases the level of judgement involved and heightens the risk associated with the appropriateness, consistency, and reasonableness of the assumptions'. The auditor has flagged it as a significant audit risk.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are sensitive to interest rates, mortality assumptions, and wage inflation. A £11m net liability is material. The full refresh of assumptions rather than rollforward means the liability could move materially either way. A lender relies on actuarial assumptions being reasonable and consistent.
findings.figures: Pension fund net liability £11 million as at 31 March 2025; pension assets £147.644 million; pension liabilities £158.952 million; triennial valuation 2025/26
findings.quote: The triennial actuarial valuation of the Pension Fund will be undertaken during the 2025/26 financial year... As this is a triennial valuation year, the actuarial assumptions will be fully refreshed, rather than rolled forward from prior years. This increases the level of judgement involved and heightens the risk associated with the appropriateness, consistency, and reasonableness of the assumptions used by management and the actuary.

findings.headline: The Sevington Border Facility has internal control weaknesses including transaction misallocation and unsupervised reconciliations.
findings.detail: The auditor identified that non-PHILIS transactions from the WorldPay account were erroneously credited to the PHILIS bank account due to a system linkage implemented in November 2024. While entries are swept out to the main account, the misallocation creates reporting risk. Additionally, monthly reconciliations between finance system, PHILIS system, and general ledger are prepared by one officer without independent review or sign-off. The council's response is to implement additional reconciliation checks, but the base problem—one person preparing and not having work checked—remains.
findings.matters: The Sevington facility is a revenue stream (described elsewhere in the plan as established and no longer a significant risk, so presumably material). Controls over it are weak: a system producing erroneous entries and no supervisory check on reconciliations. This increases the risk of undetected errors in income or balance sheet accounts.
findings.figures: Non-PHILIS transactions (WorldPay) erroneously credited to PHILIS bank account; monthly reconciliations without independent review since implementation of system linkage in November 2024
findings.quote: The audit team identified that non-PHILIS transactions, primarily from the WorldPay account, were erroneously credited to the PHILIS bank account due to a system linkage implemented in November 2024... For the Sevington Border Facility, we noted that monthly reconciliations between the finance system, PHILIS system and the general ledger are prepared by one officer but are not independently reviewed or formally signed off by a senior officer.

findings.headline: Eleven prior-year audit recommendations remain in progress; none have been fully resolved.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit resulted in 11 recommendations. All are classified as 'Medium – In progress' in the 2025/26 audit plan. Issues include: a finance team member with unrestricted 'super user' rights posting journal entries (council says arrangement is 'adequate'); investment property valuations without documented challenge to valuers; provisions calculated without formal review of assumptions; Sevington Border Facility reconciliations prepared and not independently reviewed; missing contractual documentation for pay changes; property asset reclassifications with timing and classification errors; a fixed asset register that does not support CIPFA requirements and requires manual journal workarounds; and group consolidation controls that failed to prevent balancing errors.
findings.matters: Recommendations unresolved for a year suggest either weak follow-through on control improvements or a lack of capacity to implement them. The journal control issue is particularly significant: an individual with super-user rights is also posting entries, creating an elevated management override risk. The council's response is that it considers the arrangement adequate, contradicting the auditor's assessment.
findings.figures: 11 recommendations identified in 2024/25; all 11 remain 'In progress' as of June 2026
findings.quote: From our understanding of the journal entry process control environment and the associated risk of management override of controls, we identified that one member of the finance team possesses 'super user' rights for the financial reporting system. This individual has posted a number of journal entries... Granting super user rights to finance team members inherently increases the risk of management override of controls... [Council response:] As in previous years the Council considers the current arrangement to be adequate.

findings.headline: A significant weakness in the Housing Revenue Account's financial sustainability, identified since 2023/24, remains unresolved despite recent action.
findings.detail: The auditor first reported in 2023/24 that the council had arrangements that were not adequate to secure financial sustainability in respect of the HRA. This continued into 2024/25. The council only developed its 2025-2055 HRA Business Plan in November 2025, and the auditor acknowledges that while progress has been made, this is 'only the start of the journey to address long-term HRA pressures'. The auditor will carry out detailed work to assess whether the weakness remains and whether management has implemented key recommendations.
findings.matters: The HRA funds housing maintenance and investment. A significant weakness in its financial sustainability that has persisted for two years signals either structural housing cost problems or management's inability to plan realistically. A lender needs to know whether the 2025-2055 plan is credible or a paper exercise.
findings.figures: Weakness first reported 2023/24; carries forward to 2025/26 as risk of significant weakness; 2025-2055 HRA Business Plan completed November 2025
findings.quote: there continued to be a significant weakness (first reported in 2023/24) in the Council's arrangements to secure financial sustainability in respect of the Council's Housing Revenue Account (HRA)... the Council has only recently developed its 2025-2055 HRA Business Plan and recognises that this is only the start of the journey to address long-term HRA pressures

findings.headline: Council has had disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years and cannot yet guarantee a clean opinion for 2025/26.
findings.detail: Ashford's financial statements were disclaimed in 2023, 2024, and 2025 due to the audit backstop. The auditor is attempting to regain assurance over opening balances and prior-year transactions, but explicitly states the possibility of a non-disclaimed opinion for 2025/26 is conditional: 'if we complete our regaining assurance work as well as the required work on 2025/26, then it opens the possibility that we can move away from a disclaimer opinion'. This means a fourth consecutive disclaimer remains possible.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean the auditor could not form a view on the financial statements. Three years of this signals persistent capability or governance problems. A lender needs to know whether a fourth disclaimer is likely.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued 2023, 2024, 2025; audit work performed in full in 2024 and 2025 but balances remain unassured due to backstop dates
findings.quote: if we complete our regaining assurance work as well as the required work on 2025/26, then it opens the possibility that we can move away from a disclaimer opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements

findings.headline: Subsidiary company governance: Ashford International Development Company's business plan not updated for three years
findings.detail: The business plan for council-owned Ashford International Development Company has not been reviewed or updated since the company was established in 2022. The shareholder agreement is also unchanged since inception. Audit noted additional gaps including absence of defined training requirements for board members and lack of role descriptions.
findings.matters: Three-year absence of plan updates suggests weak oversight of council-owned subsidiary performance and governance
findings.figures: Business plan and shareholder agreement unchanged since 2022 (establishment date)
findings.quote: However, the Business Plan has not been updated in the three years since that time... The shareholder agreement has also not been reviewed since it was first established in 2022.

findings.headline: Internal audit plan delivery shortfall: only 78% of budgeted audit work completed due to staffing constraints
findings.detail: Due to national shortage of local government auditors and ongoing recruitment challenges, internal audit delivered 331 of 423 budgeted days (78% of plan). This reduced overall assurance coverage, though 89% of essential and 75% of high-priority audits were completed. Cost saving of approximately £40k reflects the shortfall.
findings.matters: Reduced independent audit coverage means potential control weaknesses in uncovered areas may not be detected
findings.figures: 331 days delivered of 423 budgeted (78%); £40k cost saving
findings.quote: The audit plan budgeted for 423 days, and 331 days were delivered in 2025/26, equating to 78% of the budgeted figure.

findings.headline: Health and Safety controls rated Weak with strategic officer role vacant for four years
findings.detail: The strategic Health and Safety Officer position has been vacant since June 2022, with only a temporary post in place during recruitment. Audit identified Weak controls across H&S management, including inadequate policy enforcement, incomplete risk assessments, inconsistent incident reporting, and misaligned monitoring groups. Two high-priority actions were raised.
findings.matters: Long-term vacancy in strategic role indicates staffing/recruitment challenges and represents material governance and operational risk
findings.figures: Vacancy since June 2022; 2 high priority, 6 medium priority, 4 low priority actions raised
findings.quote: The Health and Safety work plan remains ineffective due to the vacancy of the strategic Health and Safety Officer role since June 2022. This has led to a decline in strategic planning and effective oversight. A temporary post was introduced, while recruitment for the current permanent role was underway.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision summer 2026 with Ashford costs of £150–200k unbudgeted
findings.detail: A major reorganisation for Kent and Medway councils is expected with government decision summer 2026. Ashford's estimated cost is £150–200k in pre-vesting expenses, but the 2026/27 budget makes no operational provision for this. Costs are expected to be capital expenditure but the funding mechanism remains under discussion with government.
findings.matters: LGR creates material uncertainty about future costs and diverts management focus during a period of structural funding decline. Unbudgeted costs could force reserve draws or additional borrowing, and restructuring risks service disruption at a vulnerable time.
findings.figures: £150,000–£200,000 Ashford estimate; £135m total reorganisation cost; £30m pre-vesting costs across all councils
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget does not make any operational provision or adjustments for the Local Government Reorganisation, work required in relation to this matter is expected to qualify as capital expenditure and could be funded from reserves or borrowing with discussions ongoing with the government on the appropriate mechanism for these costs.

findings.headline: Council removes £300,000 enforcement savings from budget citing unachievable targets
findings.detail: The draft budget included £300,000 of enforcement-related savings, which were removed from the final budget specifically because of 'risk surrounding the achievability', even though improved financial position meant this wasn't strictly necessary. This directly undermines confidence in the council's ability to deliver the more difficult savings required when deficits emerge.
findings.matters: If the council cannot deliver straightforward enforcement savings in favorable financial conditions, how will it manage the larger, more difficult cuts required from 2028/29 onwards when deficits force action? Questions the robustness of the medium-term financial plan.
findings.figures: £300,000 enforcement savings removed from draft
findings.quote: The saving was removed due to the risk surrounding the achievability and the improved financial position meant it was more appropriate to reset the target as part of a corporate savings strategy.

findings.headline: Deficits forecast to emerge from 2028/29 despite balanced 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: While 2026/27 appears balanced, the revised Medium Term Financial Plan forecasts a surplus only through 2027/28, then moves back into deficit from 2028/29 onwards. The current balance relies partly on a one-off £677k business rates gain from government including pooling benefit—meaning the underlying structural problem is masked by temporary favorable conditions.
findings.matters: The apparent balance disguises an underlying structural deficit. When deficits emerge, the council will need significant cuts or reserve draws, reducing financial flexibility for debt service at a time of declining revenues.
findings.figures: £285,000 surplus forecast 2026–28; deficits from 2028/29; £677,160 one-off business rates gain
findings.quote: there is now a surplus of £285,000 forecast for 2026/27 to 2027/28 before moving back into a deficit position from 2028/29 onwards.

findings.headline: Ashford receives 3.8% less funding by 2028/29 while English average increases 15.1%
findings.detail: The new local government funding formula redistributes money away from lower-assessed-need areas. Ashford falls from £24.7m to £23.8m in cash terms over three years, representing real-term cuts around 11.3%. The settlement is fixed with no allowance for inflation or service demand growth, creating a permanent structural decline.
findings.matters: This structural and permanent loss of revenue erodes the council's financial resilience and future borrowing capacity. It reduces ability to service debt, maintain capital investment, or sustain current service levels.
findings.figures: £24.7m to £23.8m by 2028/29 (3.8% reduction); national average +15.1%; real-term cuts 11.3%
findings.quote: Ashford receive a 3.8% decrease from £24.7m in 2025/26 to £23.8m in 2028/29 despite the average increase for all English authorities being 15.1% over the same period.

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: HRA has been under substantial pressure in recent years despite endorsement of 2026/27 business plan
findings.detail: Management team explicitly noted that 'The HRA has been under substantial pressure in the last few years.' While the task group endorsed the 30-year business plan as achievable, the recent difficulties and reliance on a 30-year financial model with sensitivity testing for interest rate risk show the service is fragile.
findings.matters: Housing revenue accounts are separate from general fund borrowing but still reflect the authority's asset base. Recent pressure and interest rate sensitivity in a 30-year plan create refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Interest rate identified as main financial risk; £9.5m initial annual capital works spend tapering to £4.4m from year six
findings.quote: The HRA has been under substantial pressure in the last few years, and this provides assurance that the Services is moving in the right direction.

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition costs unresolved and no reserves set aside
findings.detail: The task group agreed not to allocate reserves for anticipated Local Government Reorganisation costs because funding is uncertain. However, the management team notes it is 'unlikely that Government will provide any further funding' and expects 'transition costs should be covered by the founding authorities and savings generated.'
findings.matters: Unbudgeted and unfunded reorganisation costs represent a material contingent liability. For lenders, the absence of a plan to cover transition costs is a risk to future financial stability.
findings.figures: Amounts unspecified
findings.quote: It is unlikely that Government will provide any further funding and there is an expectation that the transition costs should be covered by the founding authorities and savings generated.

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: Budget reliance on one-off settlement windfall and pension fund gains rather than structural solutions
findings.detail: The council's improved financial position in 2026/27 stems from a £763,000 windfall from the government's provisional financial settlement and reduced pension contributions from the triennial review. These gains are being used to balance the budget and clear a deficit, but are non-recurring. The task group debated using these to freeze council tax but decided against it.
findings.matters: Balancing a budget with windfall gains rather than sustainable savings creates a structural deficit that will reappear when one-off money runs out.
findings.figures: £763,000 settlement increase; pension fund triennial review savings not quantified separately
findings.quote: This had resulted in a net increase of £763,000 compared to the draft budget.

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: Woodchurch Windmill has deteriorated due to financial constraints with unknown restoration costs
findings.detail: The council's designated Asset of Community Value has been in disrepair since 2019 due to weather damage and deferred maintenance caused by financial constraints. Restoration costs remain confidential and significant. The task group wants Cabinet to understand the full condition and costs before deciding whether to sell, lease, or retain.
findings.matters: Assets allowed to deteriorate due to budget constraints represent failed maintenance planning. Unknown restoration costs and the decision to sell or lease could involve material sums.
findings.figures: Valuation confidential; annual maintenance shortfall across portfolio evident
findings.quote: weather damage led to its current state, and financial constraints delayed repairs

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: Property maintenance backlog: condition surveys reveal more work needed than available budget
findings.detail: Condition surveys of the council's 389 commercial assets and 1,500 garages identified maintenance work exceeding available funds. With only £500,000 in annual capital budget and £400,000 for maintenance, the council must prioritise work and consider asset disposals. This creates a deferred maintenance liability.
findings.matters: A growing maintenance backlog erodes asset value and eventually forces emergency spending. For councils with limited borrowing headroom, deferred maintenance becomes a hidden liability.
findings.figures: £500,000 capital budget; £400,000 maintenance budget; portfolio valued at £161 million
findings.quote: condition surveys had been completed, identifying more required work than available funds, necessitating prioritisation and tough decisions regarding asset maintenance and potential disposals

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: Building Control service is running a £65,000 annual deficit subsidised from the General Fund
findings.detail: Building Control income is insufficient to cover costs, with a projected deficit of £65,000 in 2026/27. The service is competing with private sector providers and faces recruitment difficulties. The council is tracking deficits and surpluses in a memorandum account but has not yet implemented measures to recover full costs.
findings.matters: A recoverable service running persistent deficits points to either weak cost control or pricing problems. For a lender, cross-subsidisation from general funds masks underlying service viability.
findings.figures: £65,000 deficit for 2026/27
findings.quote: The projected deficit for 2026/27 was £65,000 with the service supported by the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Report of Overview and Scrutiny Budget Scrutiny Task Group
findings.headline: £300,000 enforcement savings target is unachievable and being removed from the budget
findings.detail: The task group recommended removing an unrealistic £300k enforcement savings target that had become a continuing risk to the budget. Officers agreed, with the Assistant Director of Finance confirming the target 'had never really looked like coming to fruition as originally intended.' This will be reset within a refreshed savings strategy.
findings.matters: Budget targets that consistently fail to materialise signal weak budget discipline and forecasting. A lender needs confidence that planned savings are real.
findings.quote: The £300,000 enforcement savings target within the 26/27 draft budget be removed to de-risk the budget but remains as part of the wider savings strategy.

findings.headline: Building Control fee income at risk due to recruitment failure and uncertain future service model
findings.detail: The council failed to recruit to a vacant Building Control Team Leader post and has extended a consultant contract through calendar year end. The wider service delivery model is under review for medium and longer term, indicating uncertainty about future service sustainability and income generation.
findings.matters: Loss of Building Control fee income directly impacts MTFP, and ongoing service model uncertainty could signal capacity or sustainability challenges that affect medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Failed recruitment exercise to Team Leader post, leading to extension of consultant contract to end of calendar year. Wider picture under review in respect of how service could be provided in medium/longer term.

findings.headline: Financial reserves of £23m forecast to decline due to MTFP drawdown and Local Government Reorganisation costs
findings.detail: While reserves are currently strong at £23m, the council expects them to reduce over coming years to support MTFP delivery, corporate initiatives, and implementation costs of Local Government Reorganisation from April 2028. The 2026/27 budget report will provide updated reserve forecasts.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility to handle unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and can affect credit rating and borrowing terms.
findings.figures: £23m current reserves
findings.quote: The Council maintains strong financial reserves of around £23m although these are likely to reduce over the next few years to support the medium-term financial plan, corporate initiatives, and potentially implementation costs of Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Maintenance budget is chronically underfunded and almost certain to be exceeded again
findings.detail: The council's maintenance liabilities have exceeded available budget for "a number of previous years" and is rated almost certain to exceed again. The council is risk-assessing all works and conducting maintenance in-house where possible, but this is managing symptoms rather than solving the structural gap.
findings.matters: Chronic underfunding forces either deferred asset maintenance (creating future liability growth), lower service standards, or continuous budget variance. Each option affects long-term financial viability.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: This risk has been updated as it is almost certain that the maintenance liabilities will exceed the available budget. This has been the case for a number of previous years. All potential works are risk assessed prior to being instructed to ensure best use of funds.

findings.headline: MTFP deficit of £441,000 over 2 years requires new savings strategy
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Medium-Term Financial Plan shows a £441,000 deficit over the 2-year horizon (reduced from £801,000 due to pension cost reductions) and £3.2m over 5 years. The council is developing a comprehensive savings strategy to address this imbalance, though delivery is constrained by the need to maintain service capability ahead of Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028.
findings.matters: A persistent structural deficit indicates the council must make permanent spending cuts or find new income sources to achieve budget balance, which can constrain service delivery or affect borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: The 2026/27 MTFP had a £3.2m deficit over the 5-year period although with Local Government Reform (LGR) due to be introduced from April 2028 the two year horizon showed a deficit of £801,000, although this has reduced to £441,000

findings.headline: Significant weakness in Housing Revenue Account financial sustainability arrangements; council lacks fully costed business plan
findings.detail: The auditor identified a significant weakness in the Authority's arrangements to secure HRA financial sustainability. The Authority does not have a comprehensive and fully costed HRA business plan that incorporates the results of the stock condition survey, the planned maintenance programme, and the financial implications of the Regulator of Social Housing's August 2024 regulatory judgement. Without these costings, the Authority lacks sufficient assurance over the medium-term financial sustainability of its HRA.
findings.matters: Housing Revenue Accounts are typically a council's largest income-generating asset and critical to financial sustainability; without a properly costed plan incorporating regulatory judgements and maintenance needs, the council cannot reliably forecast HRA viability or service delivery capability.
findings.figures: Regulator of Social Housing's August 2024 regulatory judgement
findings.quote: the Authority did not have in place a comprehensive and fully costed HRA business plan that incorporated the results of the completed stock condition survey, the planned maintenance programme, and the financial implications of the Regulator of Social Housing's August 2024 regulatory judgement. In the absence of these costings, the Authority does not yet have sufficient assurance over the medium-term financial sustainability of its HRA.

findings.headline: Material prior period adjustments to General Fund reserve and Capital Adjustment Account for both 2022-23 and 2023-24 relating to Newtown Work development
findings.detail: The Council discovered accounting errors relating to the Newtown Work development funded by Levelling Up grant. Expenditure was incorrectly capitalized when it did not meet capitalization criteria, and related financing entries were incorrectly posted to the General Fund rather than the Capital Adjustment Account. These errors resulted in material restatements to both 2022-23 and 2023-24 accounts.
findings.matters: Material prior period adjustments indicate significant accounting errors in the council's financial controls and accounting treatment processes; this undermines confidence in the reliability of historical financial data and raises questions about current control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Material restatements for 2022-23 and 2023-24
findings.quote: The Council determined in 2023-24 that the expenditure did not meet the capitalisation criteria and derecognised it from Assets Under Construction and subsequently identified that the related financing entries had been incorrectly posted to the General Fund rather than the Capital Adjustment Account. These errors have resulted in material restatements to the General Fund reserve and Capital Adjustment Account for both 2022-23 and 2023-24.

findings.headline: Auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence by the statutory backstop date
findings.detail: The auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the 27 February 2026 backstop date to conclude the Authority's financial statements for year ended 31 March 2025 are free from material misstatement. This means the auditor cannot express an opinion on the financial statements at all. The auditor concluded that possible undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on audited financial statements to assess creditworthiness and understand the council's true financial position; a disclaimer of opinion means the financial statements lack independent verification and material errors could be undetected.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We do not express an opinion on the accompanying financial statements of the Authority or the group. Because of the significance of the matter described in the basis for disclaimer of opinion section of our report, we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

findings.headline: New IFRS 16 lease accounting adds £4.4m right-of-use assets but audit work not yet concluded
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 from 1 April 2024 resulted in recognition of £4.4m net book value of right-of-use assets and £3.3m lease liability on the balance sheet. The significant gap is primarily due to peppercorn leases (little/no consideration). Audit procedures are ongoing and subject to internal review, with completion targeted by 10 February 2026.
findings.matters: New lease accounting materially changes the council's balance sheet; unfinished audit work on this area adds uncertainty to asset and liability values.
findings.figures: Right-of-use assets: £4.4m; Lease liability: £3.3m
findings.quote: The implementation of IFRS 16 has resulted in the recognition of right-of-use assets with a net book value of £4.4 million and a total lease liability of £3.3m as at the year-end on the balance sheet.

findings.headline: Council dwellings depreciation error in 2023/24 required correction; componentisation method lacks supporting documentation
findings.detail: The council improperly applied a componentisation model (70% building, 30% land) to council dwellings starting in 2023/24 without sufficient audit evidence at the time. Auditors identified a misstatement in the accounting treatment. Management agreed the treatment is incorrect and has proposed an adjustment, subject to internal quality review.
findings.matters: Council dwellings represent £432m of assets; improper depreciation methods inflate asset values and overstate financial position.
findings.figures: Council dwellings balance: £432m; 5,205 dwellings held
findings.quote: Management have agreed that the accounting treatment is incorrect and proposed an adjustment to the accounts which is set out on page 73-74.

findings.headline: Outstanding statutory objection and judicial review prevents formal audit certificate closure
findings.detail: An objection was received in relation to 2022/23 accounts. The elector has initiated a judicial review of the objection process. As a result, the objection work is paused pending the judicial review outcome, and a final statutory conclusion cannot be reached. The audit certificate cannot be formally issued until this is resolved.
findings.matters: An outstanding judicial review and inability to issue an audit certificate indicates unresolved governance disputes and may signal deeper accountability or transparency concerns.
findings.figures: Objection relates to 2022/23; matter ongoing as of 10 February 2026
findings.quote: An objection was received in relation to the 2022/23 accounts, which required our team to undertake additional statutory work... the elector has initiated a judicial review in respect of the objection process.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in Housing Revenue Account financial sustainability arrangements, continuing from prior year
findings.detail: Auditors identified one significant weakness in VFM arrangements within the financial sustainability criteria, relating to the HRA. This weakness was first identified and reported in 2023/24 and remains unresolved, suggesting ongoing structural issues with HRA financial management.
findings.matters: A continuing significant weakness in HRA sustainability is material to a council's financial health, particularly as social housing stock and HRA deficits are increasingly scrutinised by lenders.
findings.figures: Continuing finding from 2023/24
findings.quote: In summary, we have identified 1 significant weakness in arrangements within the financial sustainability criteria. This relates to a significant weakness first identified and reported in 2023/24 around the Housing Revenue Account (HRA).

findings.headline: Super-user access granted to single finance team member enables unrestricted journal posting with minimal oversight
findings.detail: One member of the finance team has super-user rights for the financial reporting system, allowing direct posting of journal entries without the standard review controls. This elevated access increases the risk of management override of controls and required additional specific audit procedures on that individual's entries.
findings.matters: Super-user access concentrated in one individual, combined with weak journal authorisation, creates single-point-of-failure risk for financial statement integrity.
findings.figures: One individual identified with super-user rights
findings.quote: We identified that one member of the finance team possesses super-user rights for the financial reporting system. This individual has the ability to post journal entries directly to the system.

findings.headline: Long-standing management override control weakness: journal authorisation system unreliable since 2016/17
findings.detail: The council's finance system does not mandate authorisation of journal entries; instead, the Head of Finance reviews them on a risk basis only. Entries are automatically recorded rather than sent for approval first. This control deficiency has been raised since 2016/17 and remains unimplemented. Combined with super-user access rights, this creates elevated risk of financial statement manipulation.
findings.matters: Weak journal controls over nine years suggests governance and control environment deficiencies that could allow misstatement or fraud to go undetected, increasing financial reporting risk.
findings.figures: Issue outstanding since 2016/17 audit (approximately 9 years)
findings.quote: This recommendation has not been implemented, and a formal journal authorisation process remains absent.

findings.headline: Material impairment of Infinity project asset in subsidiary still unquantified as of audit date
findings.detail: Management informed auditors in January 2026 of a potential material impairment on an asset under construction (Infinity project) held in subsidiary Better Choice for Property Development Limited. The accounting treatment and impairment amount have not been finalised, and auditors did not have sufficient time to conclude their procedures before the backstop date. This will be reviewed as part of regaining assurance work and flagged in VFM work for 2025/26.
findings.matters: An unquantified material impairment in a subsidiary holding property assets directly affects group net asset value and raises questions about asset management and due diligence.
findings.figures: Amount not yet determined as of report date (10 February 2026)
findings.quote: Due to information received by management in January 2026, they have made a judgement that an impairment is required on an asset under construction (Infinity project) held within their subsidiary's accounts (Better Choice for Property Development Limited).

findings.headline: Material prior period adjustment of £10.68m relating to Newtown Works funding misposts across general fund and reserves
findings.detail: Adjustments of £4.16m (2022/23) and £6.52m (2023/24) were identified for incorrect accounting treatment of Newtown Works funding, which was posted through the general fund instead of the capital adjustment account. The issue was first raised in 2023/24 but there wasn't time to resolve the other side of the transaction. This has now been corrected and will receive an emphasis of matter in the audit opinion.
findings.matters: A £10.68m restatement affecting general fund and usable reserves is significant enough to materially alter the council's financial position and borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: A prior period adjustment of £4.16m (2022/23) and £6.52m (2023/24) was identified in relation to the accounting treatment and classification of Newtown Works funding, including incorrect posting through the general fund rather than capital adjustment account.

findings.headline: Disclaimer audit opinion due to unresolved opening balance issues from prior-year backstop audits
findings.detail: The auditors cannot issue an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 accounts because they lack assurance on opening balances from the prior two years, which were subject to backstop-related disclaimer opinions. This means the auditors have not been able to form an opinion on the financial statements. The council plans to regain assurance through continued work into 2025/26.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means there is fundamental uncertainty about the financial statements' reliability, which directly affects creditworthiness assessment and the council's ability to borrow.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 28 February 2026. Prior years affected: 2022/23 and 2023/24
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous years audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 28 February 2026.

findings.headline: Regulator compliance progress slowed by skills shortages and materials supply constraints
findings.detail: Following the 2024 self-referral and C3 grading, the council has made progress on asset compliance, tenant data, and engagement. However, progress has been hampered by barriers including lack of available skills and materials shortages in the construction sector, both outside the council's control.
findings.matters: External constraints on skills and materials could delay the council's programme to achieve 100% Decent Homes compliance by 2030/31 (a core Consumer Standard). Missing this deadline or facing cost inflation to overcome supply constraints would increase pressure on the capital budget and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Target: 100% Decent Homes Standard by 2030/31; Major works spend £2,142 per property per annum years 1-5, falling to £928 from year 6
findings.quote: There has been a number of barriers which has slowed progress at times, such as available skills and materials shortages within the sector but overall the Council has seen some positive results.

findings.headline: Development and acquisition programme adds 1,070 homes in 6 years, driving debt from £45m to higher levels and annual interest from £7m to £19m
findings.detail: The HRA is pursuing an ambitious housing development and acquisition programme: street purchases (92 homes, £21m spend), s106 acquisitions (76 homes, £16.5m spend), and larger development schemes (details withheld as commercially sensitive) totalling c.1,070 homes. This requires substantial new borrowing, with interest payments rising from £7m in 2025/26 to £19m by 2030/31. Each scheme is appraised for cost-neutrality but collective programme is underpinned by market volatility, planning approval, and viability assumptions.
findings.matters: The scale of borrowing (tripling interest costs in 5 years) and dependency on development appraisals being correct creates material execution risk. Slippage, scheme failures, or adverse market conditions could leave the council with committed debt but delayed revenue pickup, pressuring Interest Cover and reserves.
findings.figures: 1,070 homes planned in first 6 years; interest payments £7m (2025/26) to £19m (2030/31); rental income £35m to £54m
findings.quote: The development and acquisition programme is ambitious, with additional stock of 1,070 forecast in the 1st six years of the modelling. This level of investment requires substantial borrowing, resulting in higher interest payments which in 2025/26 are forecast to be £7m, compared to £19m in 2030/31.

findings.headline: Rent convergence policy outcomes unknown as of planning date, with £2.9m upside/downside risk over 5 years
findings.detail: The government has announced rent convergence will be implemented but detailed terms are expected from the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025 (after this document was written on 13 November). The council models an assumption of £1 additional per week per property, which could deliver £2.9m additional revenue over 5 years, but if government announces a different level or timeline the model must be revised.
findings.matters: Rent income drives debt service capacity. Policy uncertainty of this scale (£2.9m on a £54m revenue base by 2030/31) directly impacts Interest Cover Ratio and forward-year viability; worse-case scenarios (no convergence or much slower phase-in) could force cuts.
findings.figures: £2.9m potential 5-year upside if convergence at £1/week; model assumes CPI+1% continues to 2036 under new 10-year rent settlement
findings.quote: As part of the Budget on 26 November 2025 further information on rent convergence is expected... it is not yet known what this will look like.

findings.headline: Revenue reserve is single-use contingency; any depletion requires budget remodelling and cutback
findings.detail: The HRA reserves are at a target of 10% of rental income (£4.8m-£6.9m forecast 2025/26-2030/31). The council states explicitly that if reserves are drawn down for any unexpected event or risk realisation, the Business Plan must be remodelled, likely requiring savings or deferral of investment.
findings.matters: This reserve is the only buffer against interest rate shocks, income shortfalls, or cost overruns. If drawn, the council has no further contingency and must immediately reduce capital investment or operational spending, forcing cutbacks that could breach regulatory standards or statutory duties.
findings.figures: Revenue reserve forecast £4.8m (2025/26) to £6.9m (2030/31); target 10% of rent (£35m-£54m)
findings.quote: However, should the reserve be depleted due to an unexpected event the Business Plan would need to be re-modelled to make savings, and possibly delay investment in order to ensure its continuing viability.

findings.headline: Significant proportion of debt on short-term borrowing, actively being refinanced to longer terms
findings.detail: The HRA holds a material proportion of debt at short-term rates (the plan mentions PWLB rates at 4.2% in 2025/26), creating ongoing refinancing risk. The council is explicitly seeking to move to longer-term borrowing to fix rates and avoid future rate spikes, but this introduces upfront cost and is contingent on market conditions and PWLB discount continuation.
findings.matters: If refinancing opportunities do not materialise or if PWLB discounts are removed (currently 0.6% for HRA, assumed to continue but ending March 2026), the council faces forced refinancing at adverse rates, worsening annual debt service costs.
findings.figures: Interest rates assumed 4.2% in 2025/26, forecast 4.25-4.3% 2026-28; PWLB HRA discount 0.6% at risk of removal March 2026
findings.quote: Given the HRA's level of short-term borrowing and the inherent interest rate risk that represents, the Council is looking to secure longer term borrowing as soon as opportunities arise, in order to mitigate the risks associated with future interest rate fluctuations.

findings.headline: Full regulatory inspection expected 2026/27, with outcome determining intervention level
findings.detail: Following a 2024 self-referral and C3 grading, the Regulator of Social Housing is expected to conduct a full inspection in 2026/27 covering all Consumer Standards. The council will receive an overall grading which may trigger intervention if any standard is not met. Progress on compliance has been made but barriers (skills, materials) have slowed work.
findings.matters: A poor inspection outcome could trigger regulatory intervention (management takeover, direction of asset sales, or enhanced monitoring), materially worsening credit position. The C3 grading was already a downgrade; a further adverse outcome would be material to lender risk.
findings.figures: Self-referral 2024; C3 grading received; full inspection expected 2026/27
findings.quote: The team are working with the expectation that a full inspection from the Regulator could happen in 2026/27, where the Council will be assessed across all the standards and receive an overall grading.

findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio below prudential benchmark for first 12 years of plan
findings.detail: The council's Interest Cover Ratio sits at 1.11 in 2025/26, below the target of 1.25 and well below prudential norms. The council acknowledges this but attributes it to necessary investment in new stock and compliance works. However, any adverse movement in assumptions (costs, interest rates, rental income) could push the ratio below 1.0, signalling inability to cover debt service from operations.
findings.matters: An ICR consistently below 1.25 and starting at 1.11 leaves minimal margin for adverse changes. This is the metric PWLB lenders monitor for refinancing risk. Any material cost overrun or income shortfall in years 1-6 creates danger of covenant breach.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio 1.11 in 2025/26; target 1.25; below target for first 12 years of model
findings.quote: The Council's aim is to have an Interest Cover Ratio of 1.25; however, in the first 12 years of the model it is lower than this target, but it is important to understand the reasons for this.

findings.headline: Void turnaround time at 55 days against 21-day target, eroding rental income
findings.detail: Properties are staying empty 2.6 times longer than the council's target. As of 1 October 2025, the average re-let time was 55 days versus a 21-day target, directly reducing rental income from the HRA. The council is implementing remedial actions including certificate acceleration, improved contractor communication, and process review, but effectiveness is not yet demonstrated.
findings.matters: Elevated void rates reduce rental income that funds debt service and operations. At a 0.5% assumption in the model, even modest increases in actual void rates would pressure the tight cash position forecast for years 2-3, where the model shows small deficits.
findings.figures: 55 days actual vs 21 days target (2.6x overage); 0.5% void assumption in model
findings.quote: The target to turn around and re-let a property is 21 days. As at 1st October 2025 this was 55 days.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk threatens £12.8m cost pressure if rates rise 1% above forecast across years 2-6
findings.detail: The council identifies interest rate movements as the biggest risk to financial modelling. A 1% rise above forecasts would cost £850k in 2026/27 alone, or £12.8m if sustained across years 2-6. The council is currently holding significant short-term borrowing and seeking to refinance at longer terms to mitigate this exposure. Mitigation would require reviewing the entire budget and potentially delaying the development and acquisition programme.
findings.matters: Interest rate exposure of this scale could force retrenchment of the ambitious housing development programme or require substantial reserve drawdown, directly affecting lender risk assessment and council financial stability.
findings.figures: £850,000 pressure in 2026/27; £12.8m if rates 1% higher for years 2-6
findings.quote: This is the biggest risk to the modelling, as a 1% increase in the interest rate assumptions would lead to a pressure of £850,000 in 2026/27. If interest rates were 1% higher than modelled for years 2-6 it would result in a pressure of £12.8m.

findings.headline: Stodmarsh nutrient neutrality constraint suppressed tax base growth; joint venture solution starting early 2026
findings.detail: Environmental constraints (nutrient neutrality from Stodmarsh Ramsar site) have restricted development and suppressed the council's tax base growth. A joint venture with Canterbury City Council (Stour Environmental Credits) is being created to trade nutrient neutrality credits, expected to begin operating early 2026. This could unlock previously stalled developments.
findings.matters: Development constraint is being relieved, which should improve future council tax and business rates income; also potential for planning fee income recovery; signals underlying economic constraint being removed
findings.figures: Joint venture expected to trade early 2026; potential to unlock significant development backlog
findings.quote: A solution has been developed with Ashford Borough Council and Canterbury City Council creating a joint venture, Stour Environmental Credits which is looking to start trading nutrient neutrality credits early in 2026. This solution will enable development within the borough which has far reaching benefits and will hopefully start to unlock the supply line of properties that have been restricted by the issue.

findings.headline: MTFP reliant on subsidiary company revenue streams with unquantified economic risk
findings.detail: The council has multiple subsidiary companies providing revenue to the general fund. The forecast assumes these will continue to contribute, but there is explicit acknowledgement that if the council changed direction or companies underperformed due to economic downturn, there would be material adverse impact on the MTFP.
findings.matters: Unquantified income dependency on commercial entities during economic uncertainty; no contingency identified if commercial income does not materialise
findings.figures: Commercial income growing from £2.097m (2026/27) to £7.182m (2030/31) in forecast
findings.quote: The Council has a number of subsidiary companies that provide revenue streams to the Council. The MTFP is reliant on the continued support of these companies, especially in times of economic uncertainty. If the Council changed direction on supporting these ventures then there would be an adverse impact on the MTFP and the regeneration of strategic sites within the borough.

findings.headline: Government funding remains uncertain: awaiting fair funding review 2.0, business rates reform details, and multi-year settlement
findings.detail: Core planning assumption is cash-flat government funding for 2026/27, but formal confirmation will not arrive until December 2025 (Draft Provisional Settlement) or February 2026 (final settlement). The Autumn Statement on 26 November 2025 may provide some guidance. This uncertainty means the forecast is directional only and could shift significantly.
findings.matters: Core funding assumption unconfirmed; government commitment to multi-year settlement is positive but detailed impact unknowable; fair funding review and business rates reset are overdue and could redistribute funding away from Ashford
findings.figures: Government funding assumption: cash flat 2026/27 onwards; confirmation expected December 2025
findings.quote: The Financial planning environment continues to be uncertain as the Council awaits details of a multi year settlement, details of fair funding review 2.0 and Business Rates reform which will not be fully known until the Draft Provisional Settlement in December.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing exposure of £90m average exposes council to interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council has a significant short-term borrowing requirement of approximately £90m for 2026/27, predominantly to finance capital expenditure. This is correlated to Bank of England base rate (roughly base rate + 0.25%). While interest rates are expected to fall from 4% to 3.75%, the council remains exposed to rate volatility and has not fully de-risked through longer-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Large borrowing requirement creates interest rate sensitivity; currently being favourably affected by falling rates but exposed to upside risk if direction reverses
findings.figures: £90m average short-term borrowing 2026/27, currently priced at 4.3% with forecast move to 4.25%
findings.quote: It is anticipated within the MTFP that the Councils short term borrowing requirement will be around £90m on average for 2026/27. This amount is predominantly linked to the general fund capital financing requirement which does expose he General Fund to short term interest rate risk.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation implementation April 2028 creates two-year budget uncertainty and successor authority risk
